newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S. Korea strikes push bourse to year's lowest close.
newsitem.headline: S. Korea strikes push bourse to year's lowest close.

text.p: Strikes crippling South Korean export industries sent the stock market reeling Friday to end 1996 at the year's lowest closing level, beating down government efforts to boost the bourse.
Spreading labour unrest also sparked fears that economic recovery would be delayed and the sinking South Korean won would be further dragged down, analysts and traders said.
The composite stock index ended the last trading day of the year 1.18 percent lower at 651.22. It has lost more than 26 percent from 1995's close.

"The stock market doesn't seem to be a major concern of the government," said Hannuri-Salomon Securities' head of research, Park Jae-won. "They have other things to worry about and are letting the market slip."

The nation's two largest union groups, the Federation of Korean Trade Unions and the outlawed Korea Confederation of Trade Unions, called out their combined 1.7 million members in protest of the passage of a controversial labour bill.

The legislation, which was railroaded through parliament by the ruling New Korea Party early Thursday morning, allows employers to lay off surplus workers, replace striking workers, and institute flexible work hours.

The government tried to boost the stock market this month by urging public pension funds to buy 300 billion won ($355 million) worth of stocks before the year's end. But the funds did not actively enter the market and worries about the strikes pummelled already shaky investor sentiment, brokers said.
According to news reports, strikes at automakers are expected to cost $150-$160 million in lost profits and 15,000 vehicles in lost production if lines are frozen until the end of the year.

"We haven't collected all the data yet, but we know that the strikes will be big damage to automakers if it continues much longer," said Chung Duck-young, executive vice chairman of the Korea Automobile Manufacturers Association.

The Daewoo Economic Research Institute predicted that if the strikes approach the intensity seen during 1989, when South Korean industries lost five months to labour unrest, the gross domestic product (GDP) growth could decline to 5.6 percent instead of an earlier estimate of 5.9 percent.
This year, GDP grew by an estimated 7 percent, the government think tank Korea Development Institute said.
Despite prospects of economic turmoil, analysts said the new labour law was necessary for the nation's long-term growth.

"The government realised when conglomerates like Samsung, LG and Hyundai wanted to set up huge production facilities overseas that if they didn't find ways of lowering their costs, Korea would start losing its industrial base," said Lee Jung-ja, head of research at James Capel Securities in Seoul.
Foreign exchange traders said that while the unrest has not yet affected interbank trading, the possibility loomed heavy on the won, which has been trading at its weakest levels since March 1990.
The won/dollar rate closed Friday nearly unchanged at 843.70.
